name: The Quantity Theory of Money
statement: Print more money and, other things equal, prices rise in proportion.
meaning: The quantity theory of money holds that, other things equal, the general price level is proportional to the quantity of money in circulation — inflation is, in the slogan, too much money chasing too few goods. It rests on the equation of exchange, that money times its velocity of circulation equals the price level times the volume of transactions, an identity that becomes a theory once behavioural assumptions are added.
mechanism: The equation of exchange is true by definition: money supply times how fast it circulates equals prices times real output. It turns into a predictive theory under three assumptions — that velocity is roughly stable, that real output is set by real factors independent of money, and that the central bank controls the money supply. Under those, a change in the money supply passes through into prices. The transmission is not instantaneous; it works, in Friedman's phrase, with long and variable lags, often around a couple of years.

examples.text: Germany printed money to cover its deficits after the First World War, and by late 1923 the mark was practically worthless, trading at trillions to the dollar — a stark confirmation of the theory in the extreme.
Deficit monetisation in the late 2000s drove monthly inflation into the billions of per cent, culminating in a hundred-trillion-dollar banknote.
After 2008 the monetary base ballooned without proportional inflation, because velocity fell and much of the new money sat idle as reserves — a case the simple theory struggles with.

variants.name: The Cambridge cash-balance approach
variants.text: Marshall and Pigou's reframing around money demand, holding that people wish to keep a fraction of their income as cash, which shifts the emphasis from mechanical circulation to voluntary money-holding.

variants.name: Monetarism
variants.text: Milton Friedman's twentieth-century revival, summed up in the dictum that inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon, produced by money growing faster than output.

whyItMatters: It is one of the oldest and most influential ideas in economics, four centuries in the making, and the intellectual backbone of monetarism and much central banking. Its core long-run insight — that sustained inflation is fundamentally a monetary phenomenon — is broadly accepted, and its explanation of hyperinflations is beyond serious dispute, even as its short-run and low-inflation applications are contested.

working.text: expect sustained inflation where the money supply persistently grows faster than real output, especially over long horizons.
do not assume a bigger money supply must raise prices, since a fall in velocity or idle reserves can offset it.
remember the equation of exchange is a truism, predictive only once you assume velocity and output are independent of money.

limits: The strict, short-run, proportional version fails empirically. Velocity is not stable in the short run, as quantitative easing showed when a huge base expansion produced little inflation because velocity fell and reserves sat idle. Keynesians note that money demand depends on interest rates, that a liquidity trap hoards new money, and that output is not always at full capacity. Which monetary aggregate matters is unclear, and the money supply is partly endogenous, driven by bank lending — reasons central banks abandoned money-supply targeting for inflation targeting. The theory holds far better over long horizons and for large changes than in the short run, and the causes of the 2021 inflation are genuinely contested.
misreadings: The equation of exchange does not by itself prove the theory — it is an identity, predictive only under added assumptions about velocity and output. Not every increase in the money supply must raise prices proportionally, especially when output is slack or velocity offsets it. Printing money does not always cause hyperinflation; the vast post-2008 base expansion did not, since hyperinflation needs sustained deficit monetisation and collapsing money demand. And velocity is not a constant, however stable it looks over long stretches.
origin: Rooted in the sixteenth-century School of Salamanca and Jean Bodin, developed by David Hume in the eighteenth century, formalised in Irving Fisher's equation of exchange in 1911, reframed by the Cambridge cash-balance approach, and revived as monetarism by Milton Friedman in the mid-twentieth century.

sources.text: Quantity theory of money, Wikipedia. — the proportionality statement, the equation of exchange, the history, and the velocity and endogenous-money critiques.
Friedman, "The Counter-Revolution in Monetary Theory" (1970), Hoover Institution. — the monetarist restatement and the inflation-is-a-monetary-phenomenon dictum.
Jung, "The Quantity Theory of Money, 1870-2020," ECB Working Paper 2940 (2024). — long-run proportionality and its weakening during the low-inflation decades.
